module.title: Unit 5: My Life in Music: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
module.objective: Mampu menggunakan Present Perfect Continuous untuk menjelaskan aktivitas yang sedang berlangsung dalam periode waktu tertentu, serta membedakan penggunaan Present Perfect Simple vs Past Simple dalam konteks musik dan kehidupan sehari-hari.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: My Life in Music
subModules.theme: Music, Life Experiences, and Past Events
subModules.grammarFocus: Present Perfect vs Past Simple and Present Perfect Continuous
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Music careers, live performances, and creative milestones

content.summary: Welcome to Unit 5. In this reading mission, you will explore how musicians build their careers by looking at real life stories. You will learn how to talk about finished past actions using the Past Simple, and connect them to ongoing experiences and results using the Present Perfect Simple and Continuous.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Distinguishing between Past Simple for finished events and Present Perfect for ongoing actions or life experiences.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Music-related verbs and nouns such as busking, releasing albums, and local gigs.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning texts for specific time markers like 'last year', 'since 2015', and 'for two weeks' to understand the timeline of events.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 texts about musicians and artists.
Locate specific details such as dates, achievements, and musical milestones.
Recognize and practice grammar patterns comparing Past Simple and Present Perfect.

contextWarmup.prompt: How do you usually discover new music and favorite bands?
options: By streaming music online and checking recommended playlists
By watching live street performances in the city center
By reading music magazines and physical album reviews
contextWarmup.explanation: Streaming online and using recommended playlists is the most common modern way people find new music and artists.

rules: Use the Past Simple for finished actions with a specific time in the past, such as 'He released his first album in 2021'.
Use the Present Perfect Simple for life experiences or results up to now, such as 'She has won three awards so far'.
Use the Present Perfect Continuous for actions that started in the past and are still continuing, such as 'They have been playing local gigs all month'.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Confusing Finished Times with Present Results
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often use the Past Simple when they want to talk about a recent action that has a connection to the present.
commonTrap.wrong: I played the guitar for three hours, so now my fingers hurt.
commonTrap.correct: I have been playing the guitar for three hours, so now my fingers hurt.

content.passageTitle: From Street Busking to Stadium Tours
paragraphs: Leo has always loved music. When he was fourteen years old, he learned to play the acoustic guitar and started busking in the city center. Every weekend, he stood outside the central station and played acoustic songs for passersby. He made very little money, but he gained a lot of confidence from those early street performances.

In 2020, everything changed for Leo. A local talent scout discovered him while walking past his usual spot. The scout recorded a short video of Leo playing and posted it online. Within a week, the video received millions of views. Record companies noticed his talent immediately, and a major label offered him a contract.

Since signing that contract, Leo has released two hit albums and has traveled around the world on tour. He has been working on his third album for the last six months, and he promises it will be his best work yet. Despite his huge success, he still remembers where he started and occasionally visits the station to say hello to other street musicians.

content.summary: This listening session focuses on catching specific details when friends talk about money problems and past actions. You will hear how speakers contrast completed actions in the past with current results using the present perfect tense.
learningObjectives: Catch the main topic of a spoken conversation about personal finances and events.
Identify details such as specific reasons for a problem and proposed solutions.
Notice how words link together in fast connected speech between friends.

keyPhrases.note: Used to ask someone why they look upset or worried.
Used when you have spent all your available cash.
An informal expression to show strong refusal or disbelief.
Used when finding a solution to a difficult situation.

connectedSpeech.note: The auxiliary verb 'is' contracts with 'What', and the 't' in what links smoothly to the 's'.
The preposition 'of' reduces to a weak schwa sound and links to 'out'.
The final 'd' in spend links directly to the vowel sound in 'all'.
The 'g' in 'something' is dropped in casual speech, and 'out' links to the preceding consonant.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: My Life in Music

content.summary: Practical guide on writing about musical experiences and life events using the Present Perfect Simple, Present Perfect Continuous, and Past Simple tenses.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Present Perfect Continuous for Duration
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have/has + been + verb-ing + for/since + time expression
blueprintItems.example: I have been practicing the guitar for three hours.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Present Perfect Simple for Life Experience
blueprintItems.example: She has performed live in front of a thousand people.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Past Simple for Finished Events
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + past verb (V2) + time marker in the past
blueprintItems.example: They released their first album in 2021.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'for' with a period of time and 'since' with a specific point in time.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I have played the piano since five years.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I have played the piano for five years.
mechanicsRules.why: Five years is a duration of time, so it requires 'for'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize proper nouns, including names of musical bands, festivals, and specific cities.
mechanicsRules.badExample: we saw the beatles play in london last summer.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We saw The Beatles play in London last summer.
mechanicsRules.why: Names of bands, cities, and specific cultural events are proper nouns.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place time expressions like 'last year' or 'yesterday' at the end of the sentence or at the very beginning.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He released in 2020 a new music video.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He released a new music video in 2020.
mechanicsRules.why: The time expression follows the verb and object in standard English word order.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use 'for' with a duration, and omit 'ago' when using 'for' in the Present Perfect tense.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: My Musical Journey
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences about your experience with music. Mention an instrument you play or listen to, how long you have enjoyed it, and a memorable concert or song.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I have loved acoustic guitar music for five years. I started learning chords when I was twelve. Last year, I attended an amazing outdoor music festival with my friends.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: Comparing Past and Present
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three sentences comparing what you used to listen to in the past versus what you have been listening to recently.
guidedLabChallenges.example: When I was younger, I only listened to pop music. Recently, I have been exploring jazz and classical records. Yesterday, I discovered a wonderful old jazz track.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the Present Perfect Continuous tense with 'for':
practicumQuestions.promptText: I started playing the drums two hours ago and I am still playing.
targetAnswers: I have been playing the drums for two hours.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To show an ongoing action that started in the past, use 'have been' + verb-ing with 'for' and the duration.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with 'for' or 'since':
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'since' for a specific starting point in time.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 2015 is a specific point in time when the action began, so 'since' is required.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation in this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: we visited abbey road studios in london last october
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the first word, band/place names, and months.
targetAnswers: We visited Abbey Road Studios in London last October.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns like 'Abbey Road Studios', 'London', and months like 'October' must be capitalized, along with the first word 'We'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete sentence answering: How long have you listened to your favorite band?
targetAnswers: I have been listening to my favorite band for three years.
I have been listening to my favorite band for two years.
I have been listening to them for five years.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A valid sentence uses the Present Perfect Continuous structure with 'for' and a time duration.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change this sentence from Past Simple to Present Perfect Simple:
practicumQuestions.promptText: She bought three concert tickets yesterday.
practicumQuestions.hint: Change 'bought' to 'has bought' and remove the past time marker.
targetAnswers: She has bought three concert tickets.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Present Perfect Simple uses 'has' + past participle ('bought') and typically omits specific finished past time markers.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Choose the correct preposition ('for' or 'since') for this sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: They have been practicing their songs _____ four hours.
practicumQuestions.hint: Four hours is a length of time, not a starting point.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Four hours is a total duration, so we use 'for'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fix the grammatical error in verb tense usage:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I am studying the guitar since 2021.
practicumQuestions.hint: Present continuous cannot be used with 'since' for past actions. Use Present Perfect Continuous.
targetAnswers: I have been studying the guitar since 2021.
practicumQuestions.explanation: When an action starts in the past and continues to the present with 'since', use the Present Perfect Continuous tense.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Make the following sentence negative:
practicumQuestions.promptText: He has been playing in a jazz band for six months.
targetAnswers: He has not been playing in a jazz band for six months.
He hasn't been playing in a jazz band for six months.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The negative form of Present Perfect Continuous is formed by adding 'not' after 'has' or 'have'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Form a question using the Present Perfect Continuous with 'How long':
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with 'How long have you been playing the piano?'
targetAnswers: How long have you been playing the piano?
practicumQuestions.explanation: Questions in the Present Perfect Continuous follow the pattern: How long + have + subject + been + verb-ing?

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence to distinguish between a completed past action and an ongoing one:
practicumQuestions.promptText: I wrote two songs last night. (Change to show an ongoing action of writing songs all evening)
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'have been writing songs all evening'.
targetAnswers: I have been writing songs all evening.
I have been writing songs all night.
practicumQuestions.explanation: To emphasize an ongoing activity over a time period leading up to now, use the Present Perfect Continuous.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: My Life in Music: Present Perfect vs Past Simple

content.summary: Mastering the spoken contrast between the Past Simple and the Present Perfect is essential for discussing life experiences and musical milestones at the B1 level. Clear articulation of auxiliary verbs and regular past endings makes your stories sound natural and engaging.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to sentence stress. Emphasize time markers like 'last year' or 'since 2020' to guide your listener through your musical timeline.

pillars.name: Auxiliary Reduction
pillars.target: Weak forms of have and has
pillars.explanation: In rapid speech, 'have' in the Present Perfect often reduces to /əv/ or /həv/, while 'has' reduces to /həz/ or /z/.

pillars.name: Past Tense Endings
pillars.explanation: Ensure regular past simple verbs are articulated clearly so listeners know whether an event is finished.

pillars.name: Musical Rhythm
pillars.explanation: Stress nouns, main verbs, and adjectives while reducing prepositions and pronouns for a natural cadence.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the stress remains on the second syllable when changing from base verb to past tense.
The stress stays on the first syllable for both the action and the person performing it.
Compound noun phrases often carry secondary stress on the first word and primary stress on the second key noun.
Longer words shift the primary stress to the fourth syllable from the end.

drills.focus: Present Perfect experience question with weak auxiliary 'have'

drills.targetText: The band released their first hit album last year.
drills.phonetic: /ðə bænd rɪˈliːst ðeə fɜːst hɪt ˈælbəm lɑːst jɪə/
drills.focus: Past Simple with specific past time marker
drills.hint: Ensure the past ending on 'released' sounds crisp before 'their'.

drills.targetText: She has played local gigs since she was fourteen.

drills.focus: Present Perfect with 'since' for finished duration up to now

drills.targetText: He wrote his autobiography after winning the talent show.
drills.phonetic: /hiː rəʊt hɪz ˌɔːtəbaɪˈɒɡrəfi ˈɑːftə ˈwɪnɪŋ ðə ˈtælənt ʃəʊ/
drills.focus: Past Simple sequence in a musician's career
drills.hint: Pause briefly after 'autobiography' to structure the narrative.
